paper_title: WorkFactory: Turning Professional Intents into Executable Work for Scalable Agent Training

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Scaling supervised training for working agents requires diverse professional tasks that yield reliable expert demonstrations. However, missing or inconsistent task information can obstruct teacher execution and weaken the resulting supervision. We propose WorkFactory, a scalable framework for constructing coherent and executable professional tasks. Starting from professional intents, information-level planning builds an information support graph to guide task instantiation, explicitly representing the dependencies and locations of information required for the intended outputs. Probe executions then identify support failures and guide repairs while preserving the intended work. We construct 112,686 tasks spanning 612 occupations and use the collected teacher trajectories to fine-tune Qwen models at 4B, 27B, and 35B-A3B scales, yielding the WorkPilot family. All three models improve over their respective base models across four professional-work benchmarks, with WorkPilot-35B-A3B improving from 879 to 1565 Elo on GDPval-AA v2.1. Scaling analyses reveal model-dependent diminishing returns, with execution length first increasing and then decreasing. Controlled component analyses show that planning and repair reduce probe-diagnosed task environment defects and improve downstream performance. The data and models are available at https://github.com/IQuestLab/WorkFactory.

The data and models are available at https://github.com/IQuestLab/WorkFactory. 1. Introduction Language agents interleave reasoning and actions to interact with external environments [36]. Working agents extend this paradigm to professional work in digital environments, executing workflows, coordinating tools, and producing deliverables across diverse occupations [17, 23]. This shift creates opportunities for agents to improve productivity and generate real economic value [18]. common approach to agent post-training is supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations of task execution [10, 30]. Scaling this approach to working agents requires diverse executable professional tasks spanning wide range of occupational competencies. Recent frameworks automate professional task construction by retrieving, reusing, adapting, or synthesizing task-relevant materials [12], and then collect teacher trajectories for supervision [40]. The value of scaling task construction, however, depends on whether the resulting teacher trajectories reliably demonstrate the target occupational competencies. To produce effective demonstrations, teacher agent needs access to sufficient and consistent information for carrying out the intended work. Establishing 1 Figure 1. WorkPilot-35B-A3B consistently outperforms its Qwen3.6-35B-A3B base model across four professional-work benchmarks, with representative models shown for context. this support is challenging because the information required for an intended output may be distributed across multiple artifacts and connected through intermediate calculations and judgments. For example, supplier-selection task may provide demand forecasts and vendor quotations in separate files but omit whether one vendors price includes freight. Without this pricing condition, lifecycle costs cannot be computed and compared consistently; yet providing the computed costs directly would remove substantive part of the work the teacher is expected to perform. Constructing such an environment therefore requires careful boundary: all necessary premises must be available, while intermediate and final results must remain for the teacher to derive. Otherwise, the teacher may introduce unsupported assumptions or leave essential work incomplete, weakening the resulting trajectory as training supervision. In this paper, we introduce WorkFactory, scalable framework for constructing executable tasks that support reliable demonstrations of professional work. We derive diverse professional intents by combining occupational knowledge, skill documentation, and professional artifacts, broadening the range of work that can be instantiated. For each intent, WorkFactory plans backward from the intended output using an information support graph. Rather than connecting artifacts alone, the graph captures what each output depends on and where the supporting information should be available across reused and synthesized materials, while leaving derived results to the solver. To catch violations introduced during materialization, an isolated probe attempts the task from solver-visible inputs; its diagnoses drive repairs that must restore support without changing the intended work. Only environments that pass this process are then assigned to an independent teacher, whose execution provides the training trajectory. Using WorkFactory, we construct 112,686 tasks spanning 612 occupations and collect teacher trajectories for supervised fine-tuning. Training Qwen3.5-4B [24], Qwen3.6-27B [25], and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B [26] on these trajectories yields the WorkPilot family. All three WorkPilot models substantially improve over their respective base models across four professional-work benchmarks, including GDPval-AA [4, 23] and JobBench [17], demonstrating the training utility of WorkFactory data across the tested model scales. Figure 1 illustrates the gains of WorkPilot-35B-A3B as representative example. Notably, WorkPilot-27B reaches locally estimated 1612 Elo on GDPval-AA v2.1, placing it within the range of the compared frontier models. 2 Beyond aggregate performance, we study how working-agent performance and execution behavior evolve with training-data scale, observing model-dependent diminishing returns, an initial increase followed by decrease in execution length, and changes in tool-use reliability. Controlled component analyses show complementary benefits of information-level planning and execution-based repair in reducing probe-diagnosed environment defects and improving downstream performance, supporting the value of coherent task environments for effective expert supervision. Our main contributions are as follows: We propose WorkFactory, framework that works backward from intended outputs to organize dependencies across reused and synthesized materials in an information support graph, then uses execution-based repair to preserve task executability after materialization. We conduct systematic empirical study of working-agent data scaling up to 110K tasks, characterizing diminishing performance returns across model scales and changes in execution length and tool-use reliability. We train the WorkPilot family at 4B, 27B, and 35B-A3B scales, with WorkPilot-27B achieving frontier-level performance on GDPval-AA. We publicly release subset of the task data and the model weights to support further research. 2. Related Work Agent Task and Environment Synthesis. Synthetic task and environment construction has become an important approach to scaling agent training. Software engineering provides favorable setting, where repositories offer realistic contexts and executable tests provide concrete supervision; representative systems include SWE-Gym [22], SWE-smith [35], and R2E-Gym [14]. Beyond coding, recent work synthesizes longer-horizon, multi-tool tasks through compositional expansion [29, 34], environment exploration and execution feedback [7, 28], and stateful interaction environments [11]. These advances motivate synthesis for working agents, whose tasks require coherent workspaces that integrate heterogeneous information and domain-specific deliverables. Professional Task Construction for Working Agents. NexForge [40] translates capability requirements into task directives and instantiates them through workspace blueprints, while Synthetic Computers [12] plans dependencies among artifacts to guide workspace synthesis. In concurrent work, GraphForge [31] constructs evidence graphs over real files to derive task statements and evidence-anchored rubrics, then revises these specifications using execution feedback. WorkGenesis [42] synthesizes companion materials around retrieved files and uses rubric-based failure attribution to guide revisions to the request, synthesized materials, and rubric. Whereas GraphForge compiles tasks and rubrics from an evidence graph over an assembled real-file workspace, WorkFactory works backward from intended outputs, using its graph to coordinate information dependencies and locations across reused and synthesized materials while leaving derived results to the solver. Unlike WorkGenesiss rubric-based audit, WorkFactory directly probes the solver-visible environment and constrains repair to preserve the intended work. 3. WorkFactory 3.1. Overview It first builds WorkFactory constructs executable professional tasks for training working agents. diverse intent library from occupational knowledge, skill documentation, and professional artifacts, allowing task construction to cover both established workflows and realistic deliverables (3.2). For each intent, WorkFactory plans backward from the intended output using an information support graph, which coordinates dependencies and information locations across reused and synthesized materials while reserving derived results for the solver (3.3). Because these dependencies may be lost or contradicted 3 Figure 2. Overview of WorkFactory through synthetic shipping-carton sourcing example. (1) An information support graph guides environment construction while leaving derived outputs to the solver. (2) Clean probe executions expose blocking issues and guide checked repairs before retained environments are used for independent teacher trajectory collection. Appendix C.4 provides the complete end-to-end walkthrough. when the environment is materialized, execution-based repair probes the task from solver-visible inputs and repairs blocking support failures without changing the intended work (3.4). Tasks that pass this process are assigned to an independent teacher for trajectory collection (3.5). Figure 2 illustrates the process through supplier-selection example. 3.2. Multi-source Professional Intent Synthesis Professional intents specify meaningful work before its instance-specific materials are fixed. To cover varied occupational competencies, WorkFactory draws on three different sources: (1) occupational hierarchies, which ground the work in roles and situations; (2) documented skills, which identify operations that can be composed into workflows; and (3) real professional deliverables, which provide cues about intended outputs and audiences. The three synthesis routes reflect these roles: we expand occupations into roles situated in professional contexts, compose skills when one operation supplies inputs for another, and infer plausible objectives from deliverables through instruction backtranslation [16]. An LLM-based review evaluates candidate intents from all three routes for internal coherence and feasibility, professional appropriateness, and plausibility as real workplace activities before adding them to the shared intent library L. This offline library supplies intents for environment construction; Appendix details the synthesis routes. 3.3. Graph-guided Environment Construction Constructing an executable task environment requires more than assembling individually plausible artifacts. Each requested output must be supported by complete chain of solver-visible premises, while the calculations and judgments that constitute the intended work must remain for the solver to perform. This boundary is difficult to preserve when supporting information is distributed across the user request, reused artifacts, and synthesized files. WorkFactory makes the boundary explicit before materialization 4 Figure 3. Selected high-coverage occupations from four of the 23 major occupational groups represented in the WorkFactory corpus. through an information support graph Ginfo = (Vinfo, Vcarrier, Einfo, Eloc), (1) where Vinfo contains information units, Vcarrier identifies their carriers, Einfo represents support relations among information units, and Eloc binds them to locations. Planning information support. For each intent in L, the planner starts from the intended output and works backward. It identifies the calculations and judgments behind that output, then traces each of them to the information it requires. The resulting information units form Vinfo, while Einfo records association, transformation, evidence, and constraint relations, including cases where several sources jointly support one result. In the supplier-selection example in Figure 2, vendor NPVs rely on demand and pricing information distributed across the request and reference files; together with the vendor profiles, they support the final recommendation. Each node records its content, entity and scope, and whether it is supplied, externally acquired, solver-derived, or internal to construction. The source data and commercial terms are therefore made available, while the downstream calculations and recommendation remain unspecified for the solver to complete. Grounding information in carriers. Location bindings in Eloc assign information to carriers in Vcarrier: the user request, reference artifacts, external resources, future deliverables, or internal construction requirements. They specify where information is supplied, acquired, or produced, and whether it is accessible to the solver. Internal requirements remain hidden; any task-specific premise or obligation needed for completion must be expressed in or obtainable through solver-visible inputs. In the supplierselection example, input bindings locate demand forecasts and supplier quotations in reference PDF and cost-timing rules in the request. Output bindings associate the requested vendor NPV analysis and sourcing recommendation with future cost-comparison workbook. Appendix provides detailed definitions. Materializing the environment. The planner translates the graph into an artifact-level construction plan = (𝑢, A, D), comprising the concrete user request 𝑢, artifact specifications A, and acyclic construction dependencies D. An environment worker follows this plan to reuse, adapt, or synthesize artifacts. Execution-based Environment Repair Execution-based repair tests the realized environment for missing or inconsistent support that remains after construction. The loop consists of probe diagnosis, revision, and revalidation. Diagnosing the realized environment. probe solver attempts the task using only the solver-visible request and resources, without access to the graph, construction plan, or prior execution outputs and diagnoses. It grounds reported environmental issues in inspected sources and tool observations, identifies the affected operations and deliverables, and distinguishes them from solver mistakes and legitimate open choices. Only issues judged to block task completion trigger repair; tasks without such blockers proceed to trajectory collection. Appendix C.1 details the reporting criteria. Repairing and revalidating the environment. refiner uses the diagnoses to edit the request and existing reference files while preserving the files number, types, and dependency structure; the information support graph remains the initial construction specification. For example, adding missing USD 0.15per-carton freight term for Supplier restores the support needed for an NPV comparison without performing the comparison for the solver. Each revision must pass construction checks and an LLM-based work-preservation review against the original intent and initial plan, assessing whether the core objective, essential operations, and substantive deliverable requirements remain intact. Revised tasks that fail either check are discarded; those that pass undergo fresh probe execution. The loop stops when no blocker remains or the repair budget is exhausted, with unresolved tasks discarded. Retained tasks form the candidate pool for trajectory collection. Appendix C.2 specifies the repair constraints and budget, and Appendix D.3 provides model and execution settings. 3.5. Task Corpus and Training Data Teacher trajectory collection and supervision. For every task in , GLM-5.3 [37] independently attempts the task in clean sandbox with the same task-information access boundary as the probe in 3.4. The teacher receives the current request and accessible resources, without the information support graph, construction plan, or prior probe outputs and diagnoses. The resulting interaction trace and produced 6 deliverables form an initial teacher rollout. We retain rollouts that pass lightweight filters screening for repeated reasoning, repeated tool calls, and missing or insufficiently substantive deliverables. For the 5% of tasks with the longest initial rollouts, measured by total interaction turns, we additionally apply selective rejection sampling based on pairwise deliverable comparisons; all other tasks retain their filtered initial rollouts. Each retained rollout is then converted into one or more training sequences for masked autoregressive supervision.1 Appendix D.3 details the execution settings, rejection-sampling procedure, and training configuration. Final training corpus. The final corpus contains 112,686 tasks spanning 612 fine-grained occupations and 23 major occupational groups; Figure 3 shows the occupations with the highest task shares. We collect teacher trajectories using the Stirrup [5] and the Claude Code harness [3]. Figure 4 shows the distribution of target deliverable file types, while Table 1 reports additional aggregate corpus statistics. We screen the final corpus against the evaluation tasks using request-overlap checks, manual review of flagged pairs, and file hashes; these checks identify no evaluation-task reuse or byte-identical files shared with the training corpus. Appendix provides additional details, while Appendix D.2 reports construction-time token usage. 4. Experiments 4.1. Experimental Setup Baselines. We compare the three WorkPilot models with their corresponding base models: Qwen3.54B [24], Qwen3.6-27B [25], and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B [26]. These matched base-model comparisons serve as the primary controls for measuring the effect of WorkFactory supervision across model scales. For broader system-level context, we also include three groups of representative models: frontier models, including GLM-5.3 [37], DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash [8], Qwen3.8-Max [27], GPT-5.6 Sol [21], and Kimi-K3 [15]; open-weight models (300B), including DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 [9], DeepSeek-V4Flash-0731 [9], GLM-5.2 [38], and MiniMax-M3 [19]; and open-weight models (30B), including Qwen3.8-27B [27], Nex-N2.5-mini [20], and Apodex-1.1-mini [1]. Benchmarks. We evaluate the training utility of WorkFactory teacher trajectories on GDPval [23], JobBench [17], Workspace-Bench [32]2, and OmegaUse-OfficeVal [41]. For each locally evaluated modeltask pair, we run three independent rollouts. For GDPval, we follow the GDPval-AA protocol [4] with the Stirrup harness [5]. We report official v2.1 Elo ratings where available; otherwise, using Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview [13] as the judge, we report local BradleyTerry estimates [6] calibrated to the same v2.1 scale (see Appendix E.1). For the remaining benchmarks, we use the Claude Code harness [3] with Claude Sonnet 4.6 [2] as the judge when needed and report the official metrics. Training. Effect of Teacher Choice We compare two teacher supervision on the 30K-task subset from the scaling study (4.3). The GLM-5.3 condition reuses the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B checkpoint trained on that subset; the DeepSeek condition regenerates trajectories for the same tasks with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and fine-tunes the same base model with the shared configuration. Both teacher conditions improve over the base model, supporting the utility of WorkFactory tasks beyond single teacher. The difference between students also shows that trajectory-generation choices affect how much training benefit is obtained from the same task set. Appendix E.3 details the accounting method and price mappings. 5. Conclusion We introduced WorkFactory, framework for constructing executable professional tasks to support teacher demonstrations of occupational competencies. Information-level planning specifies the dependencies and locations of required information, while execution-based repair addresses support failures exposed during task execution. Using teacher trajectories from 112,686 tasks, we trained the WorkPilot family, whose three models improve over their corresponding bases across four professional-work benchmarks. Data-scaling analyses reveal model-dependent diminishing returns and changes in execution length and tool-use reliability. Controlled component studies connect reductions in probe-diagnosed environment defects to improved downstream training utility, supporting the value of coherent task construction for scaling working-agent supervision.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: First, GLM-5.3, our teacher model, accepts only text input. Consequently, although the Qwen backbones include native vision and alignment components, we train and evaluate them only through text-only tasksolving interface. This work therefore does not examine learning from visual evidence directly. Future work will extend trajectory collection and student training to multimodal professional tasks. Second, our training study focuses on supervised fine-tuning over teacher trajectories. Future work will leverage high-quality professional tasks and their execution feedback to train working agents with reinforcement learning.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: WorkFactory trains agents to perform professional workflows and produce realistic workplace artifacts. Such outputs may be incorrect, biased, or misused in consequential settings, and should therefore receive appropriate human review rather than replace qualified professionals. Dataset and model release should also respect privacy, copyright, and licensing requirements.

URL https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.3 9325. 16 A. Professional Intent Synthesis Occupation-driven synthesis. Starting from public occupational hierarchy derived from the Standard Occupational Classification [33], we expand broad occupations into fine-grained roles. These roles seed search agent that retrieves professional context from the web as needed and generates work situations and objectives grounded in role responsibilities, business settings, and motivating events. Skill-driven synthesis. We collect documented skills from public skill directory4 and analyze each skills purpose, applicability conditions, prerequisites, and operations to derive work situations and objectives. We combine skills into candidate multi-step workflows when one skills output can supply inputs required by another and the operations jointly serve coherent professional objective. For example, quotation extraction supplies supplier cost inputs for annual cash-flow modeling, whose results feed NPV comparison and sourcing recommendation. Deliverable-driven synthesis. Instruction backtranslation generates candidate instructions for existing text [16]. Inspired by this, we use real professional deliverables collected from the web as cues for plausible work intents. We analyze their likely use, audience, content, and implied production process to derive intents for producing, updating, reviewing, or comparing such artifacts. Intent review. An LLM reviewer evaluates whether each candidate intent is coherent and feasible, professionally appropriate, and plausible as real workplace activity. Candidates that fail this review are excluded from the shared intent library. B. Information-level Planning and Task Instantiation WorkFactory represents the information required by task together with the artifacts that provide or receive it. The representation distinguishes planned output or internal construction requirement from information already available to the solver. Internal construction requirements serve only as an intermediate specification during synthesis, connecting the intended work to the request and supporting materials. They contain no instance-specific facts and add no obligations unavailable to the solver. All goals, constraints, and instance-specific information needed for completion must be expressed in or obtainable through solver-accessible inputs. B.1. Information Nodes and Relations An information node records semantic content, entity and scope, and provision status: supplied, externally acquired, solver-derived, or internal to construction. It also records carrier bindings specifying where the content is supplied, acquired, or produced. Solver-derived nodes describe quantities or outputs to be derived and their supporting relations; their values remain to be determined by the solver. Artifact Construction and Checks The artifact-level construction plan = (𝑢, A, D) contains the concrete user request and deliverable requirements 𝑢, artifact specifications A, and acyclic construction dependencies D. Each artifact specification records its role, format, required content, provenance, and materialization route: reuse, adaptation, or synthesis. The environment worker receives both the information support graph and this plan as text in its planning context, and materializes all required artifacts within single agent session. The worker reuses suitable real artifacts, modifies them when adaptation is needed, and synthesizes components when usable sources lack required information or the task requires controlled condition such as resolvable conflict. Artifact construction dependencies specify when one file needs content from another. The worker follows these dependencies as prerequisite constraints in its prompt when deciding the construction order. Other information relations remain constraints in the shared planning context and may be mutual. Programmatic checks compare planned and generated file counts and types. LLM-based review assesses content coverage and the coherence of the user request, including its references to all provided reference files. During initial materialization, failed checks trigger up to three automatic construction retries after the initial attempt, stopping when the checks pass; tasks that still fail at the limit are discarded. Passing the construction checks does not establish that every semantic dependency is satisfied; execution feedback supplies an additional check on the realized environment. C. Execution-based Environment Repair C.1. Probe Reporting and Defect Taxonomy Runtime quality assessment reports describe issues and assign severity labels. probe solver is informed that the task is synthetic and instructed to produce the best feasible deliverable. It grounds each diagnosis in inspected sources and tool observations, identifies affected operations and deliverable requirements, and distinguishes environmental defects from solver mistakes and legitimate open choices. Severity labels distinguish blocker findings that prevent completion of the minimum required deliverable, correctness findings that identify concrete task errors, efficiency findings that suggest better processes, and open observations that record non-binding risks or suggestions. Only blocker findings trigger repair, although triggered repair may also address correctness-level and other reported issues. Tasks with only non-blocking findings skip repair; efficiency and open findings are advisory. Non-blocking errors may therefore remain in retained tasks, and unclassified findings do not enter the eight-category table. 18 Table 5. C.2. Work-Preservation and Repair Constraints The original professional intent and the initial construction plan are the references for reviewing whether repaired task retains its core objective, essential operations, and substantive deliverable requirements. Minor changes to the works scope or details are permitted when restoring the conditions needed for completion; the initial plan is reference for the intended work, rather than requirement to preserve every instance detail. The refiner directly edits the request 𝑢 and the contents of existing reference files specified by A, without updating the information support graph. Its prompt requires the number, dependency relations, and types of reference files to remain unchanged. For example, adding the missing Supplier freight term of USD 0.15 per carton preserves the lifecycle-sourcing objective, whereas dropping the vendor NPV comparison or supplying completed recommendation removes essential work. This separate LLM-based review is applied after each repair, rather than during initial materialization; tasks that require no repair do not undergo it. Each revision also undergoes the construction checks in Appendix B.3. Revised tasks that fail construction or work-preservation checks are discarded. Revisions that pass are re-executed by the probe in clean sandbox without access to earlier outputs or reports.
